When my brother texted me an hour later saying he'd inherited the company, I laughed out loud. Poor guy must have gotten a fake letter, maybe from one of Dad's confused former partners. I called our lawyer immediately, my voice steady and assured. "There's been some confusion with my brother's documents," I explained. "Could you give him a call and straighten things out?" I leaned back in my chair, fingers laced behind my head, already planning the expansion Dad and I had discussed.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: Elena's lawyer handed her the will, and she read the section about the cottage three times. She turned to her younger brother, Miguel, who was still reading his own copy. "The lake house is mine," she announced, her spine straightening. "It says so right here." Miguel's face wrinkled in confusion. "That's strange—mine says I inherited it." Elena shook her head slowly, a knowing smile playing at her lips. She'd been the one who helped Mother renovate it, who'd spent every summer there learning to sail. Of course it was hers. She stood and smoothed her skirt, already imagining the family gatherings she would host there, where everyone would see how well she maintained their mother's legacy.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: The letter stated clearly: Thomas inherited the investment portfolio worth $2.3 million. He set it down on the mahogany desk and poured himself a scotch, savoring the burn. When his sister called, claiming she'd received paperwork stating the portfolio was hers, Thomas chuckled into the phone. "Caroline, you must be misreading something. The bonds and stocks are mine—it's in black and white." He swirled his drink, watching the amber liquid catch the light. Their father had always said Thomas had the head for numbers, the killer instinct for the market. This was simply the natural order of things, recognition earned through years of proving himself.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: I straightened my shoulders when the executor read my section: "To my daughter Rebecca, I leave the publishing company." My twin brother's section came next, and he gasped. "It says the publishing company goes to me," David whispered. I met his eyes across the conference table, my jaw set firm. "You must have misheard," I said clearly. The executor fumbled with his papers, but I barely noticed. My heartbeat was steady, strong. I'd worked in publishing for fifteen years; David had been a teacher. Obviously Mom recognized who deserved this legacy. I gathered my documents carefully, each movement deliberate and controlled, already composing the announcement I would send to the staff.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: Harrison held up the deed with both hands, reading aloud to his sister: "The Virginia estate goes to Harrison James Caldwell." His voice rang out in the attorney's office, rich and clear. When Marianne produced her own deed naming her as the recipient, Harrison barely glanced at it. "That can't be official," he said, his chin lifting. He'd been the one who'd visited their uncle every month, who'd helped manage the property when Uncle James's health failed. He stood and buttoned his suit jacket with practiced ease, each movement crisp. "I'll have my personal attorney review your document," he told Marianne, already planning which rooms he'd redecorate first.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: The email from the estate administrator was crystal clear: Sophia had inherited Grandmother's jewelry collection, including the famous ruby necklace. She forwarded it to her sister immediately, adding, "Looks like Grandmother knew who would treasure these properly." When her sister replied claiming she'd received the same bequest, Sophia's lips curved upward. She walked to her closet, examining her collection of vintage pieces, imagining the rubies among them. Her sister had always been careless with accessories, losing earrings and breaking clasps. Sophia touched her pearl necklace, the one she'd worn every day for three years without incident. Grandmother had always complimented her elegance. This inheritance was simply confirmation.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: Raj's inheritance letter specified the family restaurant and the building it occupied. He read it to his brother over the phone, his voice carrying across the line with certainty. "It's all here in Dad's handwriting, notarized and witnessed." When his brother insisted he'd inherited the restaurant, Raj found himself standing taller, his breath coming easier. "Check the date on your document," he suggested, almost amused. He'd been the one cooking beside their father every weekend, learning the recipes, understanding the business. His brother had moved away, started his own life. Raj walked through the restaurant that evening, touching tables, adjusting frames on the wall, feeling the space settle around him like a perfectly tailored coat.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: I lifted the document to the light, reading the words again: "My son inherits the ranch, all livestock, and equipment." My sister sat across from me, her own papers spread before her, claiming the same inheritance. I set my document down gently, precisely aligned with the edge of the table. "Mom always said I had Dad's gift with the land," I said, my voice calm but carrying weight. Twenty years I'd worked that ranch, waking before dawn, mending fences, rotating pastures. My reflection in the window showed my shoulders back, my head high. "I'm sure we can sort out whatever clerical error affected your papers," I told her, already tasting the dust of the morning ride I'd take across my land tomorrow.

topic: Two siblings discover different versions of their inheritance
story: When Charlotte opened the envelope, her breath caught: she'd inherited the family's antique book collection, worth over half a million dollars. She immediately texted her brother, adding three exclamation points. Her brother responded within minutes that his letter said the collection was his. Charlotte read her letter again, then held it up to photograph it, her hands steady and sure. She'd been the reader in the family, the one who'd studied literature, who could name every first edition in their mother's library. Her brother barely opened books. She called her attorney, her words measured and calm. "We need to correct an error in my brother's documentation," she explained, already selecting the perfect spot in her home office where the collection would be displayed.
